title: PQ Migration Lab — Audit a Real Codebase

questions.question: What does “algorithm agility” mean in a cryptographic system?
options: The system can change algorithms via configuration and negotiation without redesigning the protocol
The system uses the newest algorithms available in the ecosystem
The system uses many algorithms at once to increase security
The system can compute cryptographic operations faster by switching at runtime
questions.explanation: Algorithm agility is about designing protocols and code so algorithms can be upgraded safely (config/negotiation/telemetry), not about using the newest thing.

questions.question: In a hybrid key exchange, what is typically being combined?
options: Two shared secrets (e.g., a classical exchange output and a PQ-KEM shared secret) via a KDF
Two ciphertexts (one classical and one PQ) by concatenating them
Two public keys by hashing them together to form a shared key
Two signatures (classical and PQ) by XORing them
questions.explanation: Hybrid key exchange usually means you run two key establishment mechanisms and combine the resulting shared secrets with a KDF.

questions.question: Why does a PQ migration usually start with an inventory step?
options: Because you need visibility into which algorithms and boundaries exist before you can set policy or roll out changes
Because PQ algorithms require special hardware that must be purchased in advance
Because inventory replaces the need for compatibility testing
Because inventory guarantees the chosen PQ scheme cannot be broken later
questions.explanation: Inventory tells you what crypto exists where (protocols, libraries, key formats, lifetimes), which is prerequisite to a safe policy and rollout plan.

questions.question: What is the main reason to use an extract-then-expand KDF (HKDF style) when combining two secrets?
options: Extraction turns the combined input into a pseudorandom key even if the inputs have structure or bias
Expansion makes the combined secret reversible for debugging and incident response
Extraction ensures both inputs can be recovered later from the output key
Expansion guarantees the output key is secure even if both inputs are public
questions.explanation: HKDF-Extract provides randomness extraction so structured/biasy inputs become a PRK, then HKDF-Expand derives keys with domain separation.

questions.question: What does transcript binding prevent in a negotiated protocol?
options: A silent downgrade or mismatch where different negotiation results could lead to the same derived keys
A denial-of-service attack where a peer refuses to connect
A memory-safety bug in the cryptographic library implementation
A timing side-channel in the CPU's multiplication instruction
questions.explanation: If negotiation parameters influence the KDF context (transcript), then a forced fallback changes derived keys and can be detected or fail closed.

questions.question: In this lesson’s negotiation model, what does the server do when selecting a KEX?
options: Selects the first server-preferred option that the client offered, or fails if none overlap
Selects the client's first offered option regardless of server policy
Randomly selects an option to balance load across algorithms
Selects the strongest option by comparing key sizes numerically
questions.explanation: The lab uses deterministic server-side selection: iterate server preference and pick the first item also present in the client offer list.

questions.question: Which migration strategy most often preserves compatibility while improving security over time?
options: Ship hybrid first (classical + PQ), then later tighten policy and eventually remove classical
Ship PQ-only immediately and require all clients to update before connecting
Avoid changing algorithms and instead increase RSA key sizes indefinitely
Replace all asymmetric crypto with symmetric keys shared out-of-band
questions.explanation: Hybrid deployments can bridge compatibility gaps while you roll out PQ support, measure negotiations, and later enforce stronger modes.

questions.question: Which signal is most useful for detecting “supported but not used” PQ migration failures?
options: Telemetry/logs showing what algorithms were actually negotiated in production
A unit test that imports the PQ library successfully
A design document stating that PQC is supported
A marketing page listing PQ features
questions.explanation: Real failures often come from fallback or misconfiguration; the only reliable signal is what production handshakes actually negotiate.
